query: For refractory high-entropy alloys intended as energetic structural materials, what single testable hypothesis identifies an intervention that could improve ductility and uniform deformability without sacrificing high strength or impact-induced energy release? State the proposed intervention, its hypothesized mechanism, the improvement expected relative to the untreated baseline, the conditions under which it should hold, the prior evidence supporting it, and a decisive experiment that could falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: Adding a minor amount of boron (on the order of 0.1 at.%) to a dual‐phase refractory high‐entropy alloy (for instance, a Ti40Zr40W10Mo10 alloy designed for energetic structural applications) will promote the precipitation of fine, intergranular boride phases that enhance grain‐boundary cohesion. This modification leads to improved ductility and uniform deformability under both quasi‐static and dynamic loading, while retaining the alloy’s high strength and impact-induced energy release characteristics.
generation.material_initial_state: A dual-phase refractory HEA (e.g., Ti40Zr40W10Mo10) exhibiting a high-strength BCC matrix with energetic structural behavior but limited ductility and non-uniform deformation (e.g., intergranular fracture tendencies).
generation.intervention: Minor boron addition (~0.1 at.%) during alloy synthesis.
generation.conditions: Tests conducted at room temperature under quasi-static and high strain rate (impact) conditions, where the baseline alloy exhibits high compressive strength and energetic performance but suboptimal ductility.
generation.structural_mediator: Fine-scale boride precipitates forming at grain boundaries.
generation.mechanism: The boron addition encourages the precipitation of (Hf, Zr)B2-like borides at the grain boundaries. These intergranular precipitates improve grain-boundary cohesion and delay premature intergranular fracture, thereby promoting a transition from brittle (largely intergranular) to more transgranular or uniformly deforming failure modes. Enhanced boundary strength supports better work hardenability and ductility without compromising the matrix integrity responsible for high strength and impact-induced energy release.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the undoped baseline alloy, the boron-doped alloy should show a significant increase in fracture strain (i.e. improved ductility and work hardening) and a more uniform deformation profile, while maintaining yield and ultimate strengths within approximately 10% of the untreated values and preserving its energetic (impact-induced energy release) behavior.
generation.baseline: The untreated dual-phase Ti40Zr40W10Mo10 HEA, which, while exhibiting excellent strength and energy release capacity, has relatively lower ductility due to weaker grain-boundary cohesion.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis is expected to hold for alloys with a similar dual-phase (BCC matrix with precipitate phases) structure; results may vary if the matrix structure or key element ratios are markedly different. The effect on energy release behavior is assumed to be neutral or beneficial provided that the boride precipitation is limited to grain boundaries and does not percolate into the matrix.
generation.uncertainty: The combined evidence comes from studies on boron-induced intergranular precipitation and ductility improvements in RHEAs (e.g., PMC9572892::web::014::3_5_macro_compressive_strength_and_ducti) and the demonstrated energetic performance of dual-phase Ti40Zr40W10Mo10 alloys (e.g., PMC11767206::web::013::3_3_mechanical_properties_of_ti40zr40mo10w10). What is new here is extending the boron-doping approach specifically to energetic structural HEAs to target the trade-off between ductility and energy release, with the assumption that the small volume fraction of boride precipitation will not hinder the impact-induced exothermic response.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of the targeted dual-phase HEA (e.g., Ti40Zr40W10Mo10): one with a minor boron addition (~0.1 at.%) and the other as a control (no boron). Subject both variants to identical thermomechanical processing. Perform quasi-static compressive and high strain rate (impact) tests while simultaneously measuring mechanical properties and high-speed imaging the reaction behavior under impact conditions.
measurements: Stress–strain curves (quasi-static and dynamic) to compare yield strength, ultimate strength, and fracture strain.
Microstructural characterization (using TEM/SEM) to verify the presence, distribution, and coherency of boride precipitates at grain boundaries.
High-speed imaging and overpressure measurements during impact tests to assess the energy release characteristics.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the boron-doped alloy does not demonstrate a statistically significant improvement (e.g., >10% increase) in ductility and more uniform deformation compared with the control, or if there is a decrease of more than ~10% in yield/ultimate strength or a degradation of dynamic energy release performance relative to the control, the hypothesis is falsified.

The compressive-engineering-stress-versus-engineering-strain curves of the Ce5 at strain rates ranging from 10−3 s−1 to 5000 s−1 are shown in Figure 5a. Under quasi-static compression, the yield strength, compressive ultimate strength and fracture strain were 1000 MPa, 1367 MPa and 23%, respectively. At the beginning of loading, the alloy showed linear elastic characteristics. With the increase in strain, the resistance to deformation continued to increase and the material underwent work hardening. In this stage, internal micropores and microcracks accumulated along the grain boundaries. After reaching the highest compressive strength, the stress began to fall until the specimen fractured, at which point it was essentially the growth and aggregation of defects within the material. Under dynamic compression, the yield stage was not obvious. Instead, it was slowly unloaded in the form of strain softening after the stress reached the highest compressive strength, indicating a reduction in material plasticity.
